content.overview: Section 128 provides that the surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor unless the contract provides otherwise. The statutory illustration confirms that a guarantee of payment of a bill may cover not only the bill amount but also interest and charges that have become due. The guarantee's actual terms and the principal debtor's liability therefore matter when determining the extent of the surety's obligation.
content.glance: The surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's liability unless the guarantee contract provides otherwise; the statutory illustration includes the bill amount, interest and charges due.
content.study:
## Statutory rule
Section 128 states that the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract. The phrase concerns the extent of liability under the guarantee; the guarantee's own terms can provide a different scope or limit.

## Apply the rule
1. Identify the principal debtor's obligation and the amount legally due on the relevant facts.
2. Read the guarantee to identify what liability it covers and whether it provides a different extent or limit.
3. Identify the items included in the underlying liability, such as principal, interest and charges, and establish whether they have become due and fall within the guarantee.
4. Apply Section 128's default rule only to the liability actually covered; do not assume that a guarantee of one specified obligation covers unrelated debts.
5. Keep questions about discharge, variation, revocation, creditor securities and the surety's recovery rights analytically separate; those are addressed by other provisions in the chapter.

## Statutory illustration
A guarantees to B payment of a bill of exchange by C, the acceptor. C dishonours the bill. The illustration states that A is liable not only for the amount of the bill but also for any interest and charges that may have become due on it.

## Contractual qualification
The words 'unless it is otherwise provided by the contract' are material. Check for a cap, limited scope, excluded liabilities, conditions, or other contractual terms that alter the extent of the guarantee. Do not treat the default rule as eliminating the need to interpret the actual guarantee.

## Related provisions
Section 126 defines a guarantee and its parties. Section 127 concerns consideration. Sections 129–131 address continuing guarantees and specified revocation rules. Section 133 concerns discharge by an unconsented variance; Section 140 addresses rights of the surety after payment or performance. Apply those provisions only where their triggers arise.

sections.heading: Co-extensive liability
sections.body: The surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor unless the contract provides otherwise.

sections.heading: Read the guarantee's scope
sections.body: The statutory qualification 'unless it is otherwise provided by the contract' requires the actual guarantee to be examined. It may define the covered obligation, a monetary limit or other terms affecting the surety's exposure.

sections.heading: Interest and charges
sections.body: The statutory illustration states that where a surety guarantees payment of a bill of exchange and the acceptor dishonours it, the surety is liable not only for the bill amount but also for interest and charges that have become due.

sections.heading: Separate liability from discharge and recourse
sections.body: Section 128 addresses the extent of liability. Discharge by variance, release, compromise, impairment of the surety's remedy, subrogation and other defences are addressed by separate provisions and should not be folded into the co-extensive-liability rule.

examples.title: Bill amount with due interest and charges
examples.body: A guarantees payment of a bill of exchange by C. C dishonours it. Under the statutory illustration, A's liability may include the bill amount and interest and charges that have become due, subject to the terms of the guarantee.

examples.title: Contractual cap
examples.body: A guarantee covers B's liability up to a stated maximum. Section 128's default rule must be read with its express qualification for what the contract provides; determine the contractual limit before calculating the surety's exposure.

examples.title: Specified debt only
examples.body: A guarantees a particular loan. The creditor later claims a separate, unrelated debt of B. Identify whether the separate debt falls within the guarantee's actual wording rather than assuming all of B's liabilities are covered.

hypotheticals.question: A guarantees payment of a bill, and the acceptor dishonours it. May the claim include due interest and charges?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 128's statutory illustration says the surety is liable not only for the bill amount but also for interest and charges that may have become due. Verify the underlying liability and the guarantee's terms.

hypotheticals.question: The guarantee expressly caps the surety's obligation. Does Section 128 ignore that cap?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 128 expressly applies unless the contract provides otherwise. Interpret the actual cap and scope of the guarantee before calculating liability.

hypotheticals.question: The principal debtor owes the creditor several separate debts, but the guarantee names only one transaction. What is the key issue?
hypotheticals.analysis: Determine the scope of the guarantee and whether the claimed debt is within it. Section 128 does not eliminate the need to identify the obligation actually guaranteed.

illustrations: Section 128 illustration: A guarantees to B payment of a bill of exchange by C, the acceptor. When C dishonours the bill, A is liable for the bill amount and for interest and charges that have become due.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 128 states that the surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's unless the contract provides otherwise. The analysis therefore begins with the underlying obligation and the scope of the guarantee, then checks whether the guarantee limits or modifies the surety's liability. The statutory illustration concerns a bill of exchange guaranteed by A for payment by C; after C dishonours it, A is liable for the bill amount and for interest and charges that have become due. The rule does not dispense with interpretation of the guarantee or proof of the underlying liability. Separate questions about discharge, variation, continuing guarantees and the surety's rights after payment are governed by other provisions.
examples: A guarantee of a dishonoured bill may include the bill amount and due interest and charges under the statutory illustration.
Where the guarantee expressly limits its scope or amount, apply the contractual qualification in Section 128.
distinctions: Section 126 defines the guarantee and its parties; Section 128 concerns the extent of the surety's liability.
Section 127 concerns consideration for the guarantee, not the quantum of liability.
Sections 133–139 address specified circumstances in which a surety may be discharged; they are separate from Section 128's default extent rule.
Section 140 addresses rights of the surety after payment or performance.

keyTakeaways: Section 128's default rule is co-extensive liability, unless the guarantee contract provides otherwise.
The statutory illustration includes the bill amount and interest and charges that have become due.
The actual guarantee's scope and any cap must be read before calculating liability.
Discharge and the surety's rights after payment are separate statutory questions.
